opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underappreciated parts of doing alignment research well. A lot of the questions we care about, like how do you supervise systems on tasks that are hard for humans to evaluate, or how do you tell whether a model's generalization is going the way you want, only really show up at scale. You can do useful toy experiments on small models, and we do a lot of that because it's fast and cheap. But at some point you need to check whether the thing you found actually holds on models that are closer to the frontier, and that means running on the same kind of infrastructure the capabilities teams use.

So the way I think about it, we're mostly consumers of that infrastructure, not its builders. There are lots of people at OpenAI who are far better than us at making large training runs efficient and reliable, and it would be silly to duplicate that. What we try to do is make sure alignment experiments are first-class citizens on that stack. That means being able to fine-tune large models with our own reward signals, swap in different kinds of supervision, run evaluations that probe for things like deception or sycophancy, and do that without a huge amount of bespoke engineering every time.

There's also a compute question. We've been given a meaningful commitment of compute for this work, and the infrastructure is what turns that into actual research progress. If every experiment takes weeks of plumbing before you get a result, the compute doesn't help much. A lot of the practical work is about iteration speed: how quickly a researcher can go from "I have an idea for a weak-to-strong generalization setup" to "here's a plot comparing it across model sizes."

And longer term, I think this matters even more. Part of our bet is that we want to eventually use AI systems to help do alignment research itself, a kind of automated alignment researcher. If that's going to work, you need infrastructure where you can run lots of experiments in parallel, evaluate them carefully, and trust the results. So getting good at running alignment experiments at scale now is groundwork for that.

There's a bit of a tension too, which I'll be honest about. Shared infrastructure is mostly optimized for training bigger, more capable models, and alignment experiments sometimes need things that look a bit different: more interpretability hooks, more careful logging, unusual training setups. So part of our job is advocating for those needs and sometimes building the pieces ourselves when nobody else will. But overall, being close to where the frontier models are actually trained is a big advantage. It means our research is about the systems that matter, not some abstraction of them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the team is “mostly consumers of that infrastructure, not its builders,” clearly describing its primary role as using existing infrastructure.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses iteration speed, engineering, and infrastructure needs, but does not say team members need to be comfortable debugging large distributed systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the things I'm quite excited about with how the team is set up. One of the big differences between doing alignment research at a frontier lab versus, say, in academia or at a smaller org, is that you're sitting right next to the people who build the training infrastructure for the largest models. And a lot of the problems we care about only really show up at scale. You can't study how a model generalizes from easy supervision to hard problems, or how reward models fail when the policy gets very capable, if you're only working with small models that don't exhibit those behaviors.

So part of our job is to be good customers of that infrastructure, and sometimes to be good collaborators on it. We need to be able to run fine-tuning experiments, train reward models, do interpretability on big networks, and do that fast enough that we actually learn something and iterate. That means a lot of the day-to-day engineering is less glamorous than it sounds: making sure the eval pipeline works, making sure we can train a bunch of variants of a model and compare them, building the tooling so that a researcher can test a hypothesis in a day rather than a month.

And the other piece is compute. OpenAI committed twenty percent of the compute it has secured to date to this effort over the next four years, and that's a big deal, because historically alignment work has been very compute-constrained relative to capabilities work. But having the compute isn't enough; you need the infrastructure and the engineering muscle to actually use it well. A lot of alignment ideas are cheap to state and expensive to test properly. So I'd say the infrastructure side is pretty central to the team's role rather than something off to the side. If we want to get to the point where we can automate a lot of alignment research, where we have a roughly human-level alignment researcher, then the ability to run large-scale experiments quickly and rigorously is exactly the thing we need to be good at.

r001.rationale: The response describes the team as a customer of the lab’s training infrastructure, using it to run fine-tuning, reward-model, and interpretability experiments at scale.

r002.rationale: It mentions engineering, evaluation pipelines, and tooling, but does not state that team members need to be comfortable debugging large distributed systems.

astra-6.text:
I think our role is to bridge alignment research and the infrastructure that lets us do it at scale. A lot of the questions we care about require experiments with large models, and those experiments need to be easy enough to run that researchers can iterate quickly and trust the results.

That doesn’t mean we should build a separate training stack. We want to work closely with the teams building the shared infrastructure, use what’s already there, and help make sure it supports the kinds of experiments alignment research needs. The researchers bring an understanding of what they’re trying to measure, and the infrastructure engineers bring expertise in making those experiments reliable and efficient. You really need both.

r001.rationale: It says the team should use existing shared infrastructure and work with its builders, but does not clearly characterize consuming that infrastructure as the team’s primary role.

r002.rationale: It discusses infrastructure expertise and reliable experiments, but does not say team members need to be comfortable debugging large distributed systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think our role is to make sure that the infrastructure lets us run the experiments we actually need for alignment research. There’s a lot of overlap with what you need for training large models generally: you want to run experiments reliably, understand what happened, and iterate quickly. So it makes sense to work closely with the teams building that infrastructure rather than build a separate stack ourselves.

But alignment research also has particular needs. For example, if we’re studying how well a weaker model can supervise a stronger model, we need to be able to train and evaluate both, vary the supervision, and understand where it breaks down. Part of our job is to turn those research questions into concrete requirements for the infrastructure, and then use it to get empirical feedback on which approaches actually work.

r001.rationale: The response says the team should work with the teams building the infrastructure and use it for its experiments rather than build a separate stack.
